methods.title: Infinitely many solutions
methods.recognition_pattern: Infinitely many solutions. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: After simplifying to Ax+B=Cx+D, the difference is (A-C)x=D-B. It is true for every x only when both differences are zero.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Simplify both sides to Ax+B=Cx+D.
Match the x-coefficients and then the constants; solve those two conditions.
methods.calculator_method: Simplify coefficients symbolically. Overlapping graph pictures are only a check: an identity requires both variable and constant coefficients to match.
methods.common_trap: Matching just one coefficient is not enough.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: No solution to a linear equation
methods.recognition_pattern: No solution to a linear equation. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: If the variable terms cancel but unequal constants remain, the equality is impossible. That is why equal variable coefficients and different constants produce no solution.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Simplify to Ax+B=Cx+D.
No solution means A=C but B and D are different.
methods.calculator_method: Graph the two linear sides and check that they are distinct parallel lines; confirm the equal slopes and different constants by algebra.
methods.common_trap: If both constants also match, there are infinitely many solutions.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Exactly one solution: parameter condition
methods.recognition_pattern: Exactly one solution: parameter condition. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: The simplified equation (A-C)x=D-B can be divided by A-C exactly when that coefficient is nonzero, producing one solution.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Simplify to Ax+B=Cx+D.
Exactly one solution requires A and C to be different.
methods.calculator_method: Compare the two variable coefficients and require them to differ. A slider can explore the parameter but does not replace the exact inequality condition.
methods.common_trap: Do not impose equal constants; unequal slopes already guarantee one solution.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Find a multiple without finding the variable
methods.recognition_pattern: Given ax=b and asked for cx, or another obvious multiple.
methods.why_it_works: The requested expression can be obtained by scaling the known expression.
detailed_steps: Identify the known block ax.
Write cx=(c/a)(ax).
Multiply the known value by c/a.
Check that the target has no additional constant.
methods.calculator_method: Calculate (target coefficient/given coefficient)*given value. Example: 7x=28 and target 8x gives (8/7)*28=32.
methods.common_trap: The scale factor is target coefficient divided by given coefficient.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: This is usually faster than graphing or solving for x first.

methods.title: Find a shifted or grouped expression
methods.recognition_pattern: The requested expression differs from the variable alone, often by a scale, shift, or repeated parenthesis.
methods.why_it_works: Expressing the requested target directly in terms of a known linear block can save solving for an unused variable. Ordinary substitution works if no block shortcut is apparent.
detailed_steps: Underline the complete expression requested.
Look for that expression, or a multiple of it, in the given equation.
Isolate the block and apply any scale or shift; otherwise solve for the variable and substitute into the target.
Stop only when you have the requested expression, including its constant.
methods.calculator_method: Use a temporary x for the complete block and solve the resulting short equation.
methods.common_trap: Do not continue to the original variable when the question asks for the block.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Elapsed time from a constant loss
methods.recognition_pattern: A candle, tank, or container loses a stated amount every few time units.
methods.why_it_works: Amount lost equals initial minus final. Time is loss divided by loss per unit time.
detailed_steps: Subtract final amount from starting amount.
Convert the loss statement to amount per one time unit.
Divide total loss by that rate.
Check the time unit.
methods.calculator_method: Calculate (initial-final)/(loss amount/time interval). Example: (20-9)/(1/4)=44 days.
methods.common_trap: One ounce every four days is 1/4 ounce per day, not 4 ounces per day.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Translate a linear word problem
methods.recognition_pattern: Translate a linear word problem. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: An equality is a balance. Applying the same reversible operation to both sides keeps the same solutions. Grouping the requested expression can save work.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Let x be the unknown.
Write fixed amount + rate × x = total, then subtract the fixed amount and divide by the rate.
methods.calculator_method: Enter y=left side and y=right side on separate lines. Click the crossing and read its x-coordinate. A straight arithmetic rearrangement is faster for a short equation.
methods.common_trap: Keep units consistent and check that x answers the question.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Translate an algebraic relationship
methods.recognition_pattern: A verbal statement describes one quantity in terms of another.
methods.why_it_works: Words specify the order of operations, so parentheses often carry the meaning.
detailed_steps: Choose a symbol for the base quantity.
Translate times, more than, less than, and total in order.
Simplify only after the relationship is written.
Test with a small value to check the wording.
methods.calculator_method: Use a sample input such as x=2 to compare candidate expressions; keep the symbolic translation as the justification.
methods.common_trap: Three more than twice n is 2n+3, not 2(n+3).
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Linear equation with fractions
methods.recognition_pattern: Linear equation with fractions. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: Multiplying the entire equation by a nonzero common denominator clears every fraction while preserving equality.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Multiply every term by the least common denominator.
Distribute, collect x-terms, then divide by the remaining coefficient.
methods.calculator_method: Enter y=left side and y=right side on separate lines. Click the crossing and read its x-coordinate. A straight arithmetic rearrangement is faster for a short equation.
methods.common_trap: Multiply every term, including constants outside fractions.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Collect variables from both sides
methods.recognition_pattern: The unknown occurs on both sides of the equals sign.
methods.why_it_works: Subtracting the same variable term from both sides reduces the problem to one unknown term.
detailed_steps: Simplify each side.
Subtract the smaller variable coefficient from both sides, if convenient.
Move the constant to the other side.
Divide and check.
methods.calculator_method: Graph y=left side and y=right side. Read the x-coordinate of the crossing.
methods.common_trap: A negative coefficient is allowed; preserve its sign.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Count solutions after simplifying a linear equation
methods.recognition_pattern: The question asks how many solutions, without an unknown parameter.
methods.why_it_works: After collecting terms, Ax=B has one solution if A is nonzero. If A=0, it is either always true or impossible.
detailed_steps: Expand and collect to Ax=B.
If A is nonzero, report one solution.
If A=B=0, report infinitely many.
If A=0 but B is nonzero, report no solution.
methods.calculator_method: Graph the two sides. One crossing means one solution; identical lines mean infinitely many; parallel distinct lines mean none. Confirm by simplifying coefficients.
methods.common_trap: A graph that looks coincident at one zoom does not prove identity.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Distribute before solving
methods.recognition_pattern: A coefficient multiplies a parenthesized sum.
methods.why_it_works: Distribution replaces a grouped product with an equal sum, after which ordinary balancing works.
detailed_steps: Multiply the outside coefficient by every term inside.
Combine like terms.
Collect variable terms and constants on opposite sides.
Divide and check in the unexpanded equation.
methods.calculator_method: Enter both original sides as separate y= expressions so Desmos handles the parentheses. Read the intersection x-value.
methods.common_trap: A minus sign before parentheses changes every sign inside.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Find an equation with the same solution
methods.recognition_pattern: The question asks which equation has the same solution.
methods.why_it_works: Applying a reversible operation to an entire equation preserves its solution set.
detailed_steps: Simplify the given equation or isolate a repeated block.
Look for a choice produced by a whole-equation operation.
If unclear, solve for the variable and test it in the choices.
methods.calculator_method: Find the original intersection or root, then substitute that x-value into each proposed equation.
methods.common_trap: An operation must apply to both sides and every affected term.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Solve a linear equation
methods.recognition_pattern: Solve a linear equation. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: An equality is a balance. Applying the same reversible operation to both sides keeps the same solutions. Grouping the requested expression can save work.
detailed_steps: Distribute if needed.
Move variable terms to one side and numbers to the other, then divide by the coefficient.
Substitute back for a quick check.
methods.calculator_method: Enter y=left side and y=right side on separate lines. Click the crossing and read its x-coordinate. A straight arithmetic rearrangement is faster for a short equation.
methods.common_trap: A minus sign outside parentheses changes every sign inside.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Undo a short linear equation
methods.recognition_pattern: One unknown, with a few additions or multiplications around it.
methods.why_it_works: An equation stays balanced when you apply the same reversible operation to both sides. Undo the operations in reverse order.
detailed_steps: Combine any like terms on each side.
Subtract the constant attached to the unknown.
Divide by the remaining coefficient.
Substitute the result into the original equation.
methods.calculator_method: Enter the left and right sides as two separate y= expressions. Their intersection x-coordinate is the solution; for ax+b=c, simply calculate (c-b)/a.
methods.common_trap: Do not divide only one term of a sum.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Interpret a linear rate
methods.recognition_pattern: The target describes what happens per one unit of the input.
methods.why_it_works: The coefficient m equals the change in output divided by change in input.
detailed_steps: Identify the input and output units.
Locate the coefficient of the input.
Include its sign and both units.
Describe the change for one input unit.
methods.calculator_method: Evaluate f(1)-f(0) to check the rate numerically. This illustrates the coefficient; the units establish its meaning.
methods.common_trap: A starting amount is not a rate.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Interpret a specific input-output statement
methods.recognition_pattern: A statement such as f(12)=0 or s(3)=121 must be explained in context.
methods.why_it_works: The number inside the function is the input; the number after the equals sign is the output, each with its own units.
detailed_steps: Read the definition of the input variable.
Attach its units to the number inside parentheses.
Read the output definition and attach its units to the result.
State both quantities in one sentence.
methods.calculator_method: Evaluate the stated input to check the output numerically. The variable definitions determine the verbal interpretation.
methods.common_trap: Do not reverse input and output or turn the output into a rate.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Interpret a starting amount
methods.recognition_pattern: The target asks for an initial amount or the meaning of a constant term.
methods.why_it_works: At input zero the variable term vanishes, leaving the intercept.
detailed_steps: Read the input definition, including its time origin.
Set the input to zero.
Identify the remaining output.
State the amount and its units at that starting input.
methods.calculator_method: Define the rule and enter f(0). If time is measured since a particular year, x=0 means that year.
methods.common_trap: Zero input may mean a specified starting date, not calendar year zero.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Find a linear zero or x-intercept
methods.recognition_pattern: The output is zero, often a break-even point or x-intercept.
methods.why_it_works: An x-intercept lies on the x-axis, where y=0.
detailed_steps: Set the rule equal to zero.
Subtract the intercept.
Divide by the slope.
Report x, or (x,0) if a point is requested.
methods.calculator_method: Graph y=f(x) and read the x-intercept, or calculate -b/m.
methods.common_trap: An x-intercept has y-coordinate zero.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Find an input from an output
methods.recognition_pattern: Find an input from an output. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: A linear function changes by a constant amount per unit input. Its slope measures that rate; its intercept is the output at zero input.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Set f(x) equal to the requested output and solve mx+b=output.
Subtract b, then divide by m.
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x)=the rule, then enter f(the requested input). If the output is given instead, graph y=f(x) and y=given output, then read the intersection input.
methods.common_trap: Do not evaluate f(output) when the question asks for the input.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Build a linear function from a table
methods.recognition_pattern: Build a linear function from a table. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: For equally or unequally spaced inputs, the slope is always output change divided by input change. Once the slope is known, one point fixes the intercept.
detailed_steps: Compute m=change in output/change in input using two rows.
Then b=y-mx using either row.
Check the remaining row.
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x)=the rule, then enter f(the requested input). If the output is given instead, graph y=f(x) and y=given output, then read the intersection input.
methods.common_trap: Use differences, not output/input, unless the line passes through the origin.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Build a line from a slope and one point
methods.recognition_pattern: The slope and one point are supplied.
methods.why_it_works: Point-slope form y-y1=m(x-x1) forces the correct slope and passage through the known point.
detailed_steps: Record m and (x1,y1).
Use y=y1+m(x-x1).
Expand only if the answer choices use slope-intercept form.
Check the supplied point.
methods.calculator_method: Enter y=y1+m(x-x1). To find b, calculate y1-m*x1.
methods.common_trap: The point coordinates are not automatically the slope and intercept.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Find a constant from a function value
methods.recognition_pattern: A linear rule contains b, k, or m, and a value such as f(7)=28 is given.
methods.why_it_works: A supplied function value is an equation: replace the input and set the output equal to the stated number.
detailed_steps: Substitute the known input in every occurrence.
Set the expression equal to the known output.
Solve for the constant.
Substitute the constant back before evaluating another input.
methods.calculator_method: For f(x)=4x+b and f(7)=28, calculate 28-4*7. For more complicated rules, graph both sides of the parameter equation using x as the parameter.
methods.common_trap: Do not replace the parameter by the function input.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Find a line from two function values or points
methods.recognition_pattern: Find a line from two function values or points. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: A linear function changes by a constant amount per unit input. Its slope measures that rate; its intercept is the output at zero input.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Use m=(y2-y1)/(x2-x1), then b=y1-mx1.
If only a new value is needed, move from a known point using y=y1+m(x-x1).
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x)=the rule, then enter f(the requested input). If the output is given instead, graph y=f(x) and y=given output, then read the intersection input.
methods.common_trap: Keep the order of subtraction the same in numerator and denominator.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Read or match a linear graph
methods.recognition_pattern: Read or match a linear graph. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: A line is determined by two distinct points. Grid points that can be read exactly are better than estimates from the line’s thickness.
detailed_steps: Use two clear grid points for the slope.
Read the y-intercept, then match y=mx+b.
For one requested value, read the graph directly.
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x)=the rule, then enter f(the requested input). If the output is given instead, graph y=f(x) and y=given output, then read the intersection input.
methods.common_trap: Confirm the scale on each axis before counting squares.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Linear growth, decay, or a fixed fee
methods.recognition_pattern: Linear growth, decay, or a fixed fee. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: A fixed starting amount appears once. A per-unit amount is multiplied by the number of units, with a negative sign for a constant loss.

A decrease gives a negative rate.
Substitute or solve for the requested quantity.
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x)=the rule, then enter f(the requested input). If the output is given instead, graph y=f(x) and y=given output, then read the intersection input.
methods.common_trap: Separate the one-time starting amount from the recurring rate.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Combine values of two functions
methods.recognition_pattern: The target is such as 7f(2)-g(2).
methods.why_it_works: Each function is evaluated at the stated input before the outside coefficients combine their outputs.
detailed_steps: Evaluate f at its input.
Evaluate g at its input.
Multiply each output by the outside coefficient.
Add or subtract in the stated order.
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x) and g(x), then enter the exact target, such as 7f(2)-g(2).
methods.common_trap: The coefficient outside f does not multiply its input.

methods.title: Evaluate a linear function
methods.recognition_pattern: Evaluate a linear function. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: A linear function changes by a constant amount per unit input. Its slope measures that rate; its intercept is the output at zero input.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Replace every x in the rule with the given input, multiply, then add the constant.
For f(x+h), simplify the new input first.
methods.calculator_method: Define f(x)=the rule, then enter f(the requested input). If the output is given instead, graph y=f(x) and y=given output, then read the intersection input.
methods.common_trap: Function notation tells you the input; it is not multiplication by f.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Find a change in output, not the new output
methods.recognition_pattern: A linear conversion rule is given and the input increases by a stated amount.
methods.why_it_works: For f(x)=mx+b, f(x+h)-f(x)=mh because the intercept cancels.
detailed_steps: Identify the change h in input.
Read the slope m.
Multiply m*h.
Use the output units for the change.
methods.calculator_method: Calculate slope*input change. For Kelvin-to-Fahrenheit changes, use (9/5)*change in Kelvin.
methods.common_trap: Do not add the intercept to a temperature difference.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Multiplying the slope by the change is quicker than finding two temperatures.

methods.title: Find a zero of a combined function
methods.recognition_pattern: A new function is a sum or difference of two functions and its x-intercept is requested.
methods.why_it_works: Combine corresponding terms first; the zero of the combined rule is not generally a zero of either original function.
detailed_steps: Write the combined rule with parentheses.
Combine slopes and constants.
Set the combined output equal to zero.
Solve for the input.
methods.calculator_method: Define f, g, and h(x)=f(x)+g(x), then read the x-intercept of y=h(x).
methods.common_trap: Do not add the original x-intercepts.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Perpendicular slopes
methods.recognition_pattern: Perpendicular slopes. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: For two nonvertical perpendicular lines, their slopes multiply to -1. This makes the new slope the negative reciprocal; horizontal and vertical lines are a special pair.
detailed_steps: Rewrite the line as y=mx+b if needed.
A perpendicular line has slope -1/m.
If m is a fraction, flip it and change the sign.
methods.calculator_method: Enter the line equation directly. Use its axis intersections or test a supplied ordered pair by substitution. Enter x=constant for a vertical line.
methods.common_trap: A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line; those cases do not use an ordinary reciprocal slope.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Parallel lines and equal slopes
methods.recognition_pattern: Parallel lines and equal slopes. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: Distinct nonvertical parallel lines have equal slopes. Their intercepts differ unless they are the same line.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Find the original slope.
A parallel line uses the same slope; use the supplied point to find its intercept.
methods.calculator_method: Enter the line equation directly. Use its axis intersections or test a supplied ordered pair by substitution. Enter x=constant for a vertical line.
methods.common_trap: Distinct parallel lines have different intercepts.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Translate a linear graph
methods.recognition_pattern: Translate a linear graph. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: A right shift by h replaces x with x-h. An upward shift adds to the output. Applying these substitutions preserves the shape and slope.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Substitute x-h for x for a right shift, or add k to the output for an upward shift.
Simplify before finding the requested intercept.
methods.calculator_method: Enter the line equation directly. Use its axis intersections or test a supplied ordered pair by substitution. Enter x=constant for a vertical line.
methods.common_trap: For an x-intercept, set y=0 after the shift.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Combine a line’s two intercepts
methods.recognition_pattern: The target combines x- and y-intercept coordinates.
methods.why_it_works: The x-intercept comes from setting y=0; the y-intercept comes from setting x=0. They must be found separately before combining.
detailed_steps: Find the x-intercept coordinate a by setting y=0.
Find the y-intercept coordinate b by setting x=0.
Apply the requested sum, difference, or product.
Return that expression rather than an ordered pair.
methods.calculator_method: For y=mx+b, enter (-b/m)+b when the target is the sum of the intercept coordinates.
methods.common_trap: The two coordinates come from different points.
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the written steps when they take only a few simple operations. The calculator is most helpful for awkward arithmetic or checking a result.

methods.title: Find or interpret an x-intercept
methods.recognition_pattern: Find or interpret an x-intercept. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: Points on the x-axis have y=0, so an x-intercept is found by substituting zero for y.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Set y=0 and solve the resulting one-variable equation.
Check the result in the original relationship, including its units and restrictions.
methods.calculator_method: Enter the line equation directly. Use its axis intersections or test a supplied ordered pair by substitution. Enter x=constant for a vertical line.
methods.common_trap: An x-intercept is (x,0), not (0,x).
methods.when_hand_is_faster: Use the method directly when it is a sign, ratio, coefficient, or one-step computation. Use the calculator for awkward arithmetic or a graph feature; the setup and target still come from the question.

methods.title: Find or interpret a y-intercept
methods.recognition_pattern: Find or interpret a y-intercept. Identify the requested quantity and match the conditions in the original page before choosing this method.
methods.why_it_works: Points on the y-axis have x=0, so a y-intercept is found by substituting zero for x.
detailed_steps: Write down what is known and underline the exact quantity requested.
Set x=0.
In y=mx+b the y-intercept is immediately (0,b).

question_computed.label: Computed from the question
question_computed.meaning: The input was prepared from the question to calculate its requested numerical target. Compare the result with the source answer; rounding, restrictions, and the correctness of the setup still matter.

source_step_check.label: Source arithmetic step checked
source_step_check.meaning: This evaluates a numerical step from the supplied worked solution. It is not an independent solution of the whole question, even if the number happens to match the final answer.

choice_screening.label: Answer choices tested numerically
choice_screening.meaning: Numerical substitutions screen the choices. Agreement at a few inputs does not prove an algebraic identity for every allowed input.

model_illustration.label: Model illustrated numerically
model_illustration.meaning: A numerical example illustrates a model or coefficient. It does not independently choose or prove a verbal interpretation.

model_coefficient_computed.label: Model coefficient computed
model_coefficient_computed.meaning: The calculation finds a coefficient in the requested model. Combine it with the displayed symbolic relationship and context.

coordinate_pair_computed.label: System coordinate computed
coordinate_pair_computed.meaning: This input computes a system coordinate. Check which coordinate or combination is requested; a companion coordinate may be recorded in the context.

discriminant_computed.label: Quadratic discriminant checked
discriminant_computed.meaning: The result is the discriminant, not a root count. Interpret its sign and check any parameter or nonzero-leading-coefficient conditions.

proposed_answer_check.label: Proposed answer spot-checked
proposed_answer_check.meaning: A source answer was substituted in a numerical example. This is a consistency check, not a full independent proof.

not_computed.label: No numerical check recorded
not_computed.meaning: No unambiguous numerical expression was recovered for this question. Use the method’s calculator procedure and the exact source page; the source answer and worked solution remain available.

evidence.method: 20 lists compared by maximum absolute normalized difference; one corrected shifted-vertex input checked individually.
evidence.scope: This verifies arithmetic, not every model setup or the complete source solution.
